body: Note: I noticed the scroll position isn't restored for the same page navigation, and this is different from normal reload. Is this an intended difference to conform something, or just implemented like this?
That should probably be handled inside the navigate algorithm. Might not be covered at the moment.

This is a bit tricky to fix due to spec-structure reasons. Namely, currently "entry update" is something you initiate the navigate algorithm with; a few special callers use it (location.reload and UI reload). However, it seems like this is a general property of navigation, that any time you navigate to the same URL, you should perform an entry update.

So I think the correct fix here is to completely remove the concept of entry update, and replace it with a URL comparison. @annevk, it seems like this is kind of big and worth fixing; you up for it?

Thanks.

Now, I'm changing Chrome's same page navigation behavior to restore scroll position, scale factor, and so on as we do for usual reloads. This is for efforts to reduce unnecessary reload variants that have minor differences just for historical or no reason.
@smaug---- does https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1742#issuecomment-246461191 match your understanding of navigation?
@smaug---- friendly ping.

http://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/d1276b5b84e6cf7991c8e640b5e0ffffd54575a6/docshell/base/nsDocShell.cpp#11558-11560,11580-11591,11597,11603
is where Gecko does the same uri check. So, same uri becomes a replacement load in session history.
That does not preserve scroll position or such, since it is still a new load. I think that behavior makes sense.  location.href = location.href; is not the same as location.reload();

I'm not sure I like the replacement in session history behavior, since it is rather magical special case, but we can't change that historical  behavior, I believe.

Some relevant bugs in Gecko:
https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=90098
https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=83684
https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=300805
Can you explain why you think it's valuable to distinguish between `location.reload()` and `location.href = location.href`? I've seen at least one page teaching those to authors as equivalent.

I have another related question that someone here may know.

Did we have any historical reason why standardized location.reload() did not take a boolean argument?
If there wasn't a strong reason, I may want to make an interface change on Chrome so that location.reload() takes a boolean as Firefox does.

This is also related to the change I made for user-initiated reloads on Chrome. Now Chrome was changed to validate only main resources, and follow the protocol for other resources when users initiates reloads from user interfaces. I'm going to adopt the same behavior for location.reload() to make things consistent. But, I have a bit concern that users may need a way to force to validate all resources from JavaScript.

I don't know of any such argument against it. Although it would be a bit sad to move from a 3/1 browser split to a 2/2 browser split.

It would be good to fix the original bug posted here. I guess we didn't do a full investigation of what all the different browsers do. We should survey the various ways of reloading and see if there are differences between them, with the understanding that Chrome wants to minimize differences whereas per @smaug---- Gecko wants to have at least two modes (one that restores scroll position and one that does not). If we can find a browser majority to converge on in the spec then we can fix this.

(Although, maybe we should first just fix it with the Chrome-preferred behavior of a single reload mode, because that is simple and right now the spec is super-broken in that it wipes out all future history entries.)

@toyoshim please file a new issue on `location.reload()` taking another argument if you still wish to pursue that. Note that it has been discussed before and dismissed: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1037721 (also has pointers to standards discussion).
@annevk given that this bit @bzbarsky, who filed #2084, are you up for fixing it?

> Can you explain why you think it's valuable to distinguish between location.reload() and location.href = location.href? Both Chrome and Firefox exhibit this behavior actually. It was actually harder to reproduce in Firefox since if you directly grab window.scrollY after a reload it returns the wrong number. But with a timeout it returns the same thing as Chrome. Here's the demo I created (not quite sure how to turn it into a test): ``` Navigate to the same URL using location.href and location.reload()
``` So it seems that for same-URL you want to replace the history entry and for reload you want to update it. I also think that behavior makes sense. When I reload I expect scrolling to be preserved.

So it seems that "entry update" is something we need to keep.

But in addition we might need to have a check if the URL is the same as that of the browsing context's active document and it's not an "entry update": in that case we replace the browsing context's current entry with a new entry.

And that is different from the normal case as any forward-history (entries after the current entry) would not be removed.

Does that make sense to everyone?

(Although what @bzbarsky suggests in #2084 would be more like setting the "replacement enabled flag" at the start of "update the session history with the new page", if the URL is the URL of the browsing context's active document and the browsing context's current entry's URL, and thereby remove forward-history.)

Am I correct that the plan is then that https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#update-the-session-history-with-the-new-page step 2 splits into three cases: entry update, same-URL-but-not-entry-update, and otherwise? That sounds reasonable, although I would slightly prefer we align with @toyoshim's quest to bring this down to two cases.

> I would slightly prefer we align with @toyoshim's quest to bring this down to two cases.

Edge only returns 0, 0 for https://jsbin.com/jofuli/edit?html,console,output; I don't have my Safari Tech Preview computer.

Go to https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/ in a browser. Page down a bunch. Refresh through the UI or a keyboard shortcut. It'll restore the scroll position. It seems weird for `location.refresh()` to not match that and I'd be very surprised if Chrome actually wanted to abandon that behavior.
Right, as per https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1742#issuecomment-246587787, @toyoshim wants to always restore scroll position.
Okay, I think that should be a distinct issue as that requires implementer interest from more than one party. We'd be going from fixing a spec bug to also introducing new behavior.

(Although it belongs in that new issue, posting it here so I don't forget. If you scroll down on https://www.w3.org/ and hit "Home", I don't think users would expect that the scroll position would be retained.)

> Although what @bzbarsky suggests in #2084 would be more like setting the "replacement enabled flag" at the start of "update the session history with the new page", if the URL is the URL of the browsing context's active document and the browsing context's current entry's URL, and thereby remove forward-history.

Forward-history shouldn't get removed here, afaict.  Is it removed in any browsers?

I don't know. I guess I should try to test. But you suggested that "replacement enabled" was all there is to it, but that would in fact cause forward-history removal.

I think instead what we need to do is outlined in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1742#issuecomment-262795000. And then if all browsers are indeed convinced that refresh and same-URL navigation should behave identically and implement that we could remove the third variant, but that should be tracked separately.

> But you suggested that "replacement enabled" was all there is to it, but that would in fact cause forward-history removal.

I just tested the behavior of `location.replace` in Firefox, Chrome, and Safari as follows:

1. Load http://web.mit.edu
2. Load https://news.ycombinator.com/
3. Hit the back button.
4. Evaluate `location.replace("http://example.com")` in the console.

In all three, forward history is _not_ removed.  So I'm quite surprised that "replacement enabled" would lead to forward history removal in the spec, ever.  Apart from location.replace and loads coming from initial about:blank (for which there is no forward history around), are there other cases that involve "replacement enabled"?  I guess some of the "navigate before the load is done" cases?

Sorry, I should have been more clear. In https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#update-the-session-history-with-the-new-page if you don't pass a "entry update" flag of some kind forward history is removed. So you suggesting "replacement enabled" is all there is to it led me down the path of thinking you meant no "entry update" of some kind. Anyway, I'm pretty confident that's all a misunderstanding and we need to do https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1742#issuecomment-262795000 as I said.
